items.title: Claude Now Lets You Install Artifacts as Desktop Apps
items.summary: Anthropic has released a new feature for Claude that allows users to install artifacts as desktop apps on macOS and Windows. Artifacts are documents, designs, dashboards, and interactive tools that Claude creates in a panel alongside your chat, where you can view and edit them. When you ask Claude t…
items.body: Anthropic has released a new feature for Claude that allows users to install artifacts as desktop apps on macOS and Windows. Artifacts are documents, designs, dashboards, and interactive tools that Claude creates in a panel alongside your chat, where you can view and edit them. When you ask Claude to create an artifact, you can now click "Install as app" in the Share menu, after which you'll be able to launch it in its own dedicated app window and see it in the Dock. Artifact-based apps don't need to be packaged or signed, but they do need a permission level to be set. Choosing Default permissions means they can only do what they'd be able to do in a browser, while giving them higher App permissions means they can do things like create always-on-top windows, listen for global keyboard shortcuts, and send notifications. Full computer access means apps can run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. Apps can be used with connectors, and they include an option to add a menu bar item. Apps also update automatically when the underlying artifact is edited, and each change prompts a new permissions request. Anthropic has made some example apps available to try and to give users an idea of what's possible. Anthropic says building an app and any calls it makes to Claude count toward usage limits. The feature remains in beta and is available on all plans in Claude Desktop, though Enterprise users will need to switch it on manually first. items.title: Tidal Bans AI Music, While Apple Music Sticks to Labels
items.summary: Streaming music service Tidal today said it plans to start blocking AI music on December 9. Any track generated entirely with AI will be removed from the platform, with Tidal rejecting AI songs in the future. Tidal lead Robert Andersen said 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days have been…
items.body: Streaming music service Tidal today said it plans to start blocking AI music on December 9. Any track generated entirely with AI will be removed from the platform, with Tidal rejecting AI songs in the future. Tidal lead Robert Andersen said 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days have been flagged as AI-generated. Approximately 29 million songs will be deleted and Tidal expects 80,000 to 85,000 songs to be rejected per day. AI music will start disappearing on December 9 and will be "completely gone" at the beginning of 2027. AI-assisted music will continue to be allowed, since the policy is only for songs made entirely with AI tools. Tidal previously demonetized AI music, but removing it goes a step further. Andersen said Tidal believes the move will "resonate with both artists and listeners alike" because 96 percent of AI songs get zero plays. Apple hasn't banned AI songs from Apple Music , but it introduced AI Transparency Tags earlier this year. Apple is relying on labels and distributors to disclose when AI has been used, and it said in August that tracks "materially generated using AI" must have a "Made With AI" label. In April, ‌Apple Music‌ VP Oliver Schusser said that more than a third of monthly uploads to ‌Apple Music‌ are 100 percent AI-generated, but AI music accounted for less than 0.5 percent of actual listening. items.title: Add Holiday Lights and Snow to Your Mac With Festivitas
items.summary: Festivitas is a fun little holiday-themed Mac app that developer Simon Støvring introduced two years ago and has been updating since. Its main purpose is to add lights to the Mac's Dock and menu bar, but there's also a version for the iPhone and iPad . The holiday 2026 Festivitas update adds new cus…
items.body: Festivitas is a fun little holiday-themed Mac app that developer Simon Støvring introduced two years ago and has been updating since. Its main purpose is to add lights to the Mac's Dock and menu bar, but there's also a version for the iPhone and iPad . The holiday 2026 Festivitas update adds new customizations. For the first time, you can upload custom bulb shapes. There's an option to import an image and convert it to a bulb in a string of lights. Simple PNGs on a transparent background produce the best results, and for more complex images, bulbs can use the original colors. You can customize light shapes, color, size, opacity, drop height, cable thickness, and more in the Settings. Lights can animate with different patterns, like pulse, twinkle, chase, and wave. There are pointer decorations like sparkles, bubbles, falling leaves, confetti, a Christmas tree, a wreath, and more. Falling snow will now pile up on top of app windows for an added holiday effect. You can adjust snow rate, density, and flake size. Snow and lights can be displayed above app windows or just on the desktop, with lights also visible on the Dock. Shortcuts can be used to play music and turn on lights, activate the snow effect if the weather forecast includes snow, and start a snowstorm. Along with custom bulb shapes and falling snow, Festivitas for the iPhone and ‌iPad‌ now fully transparent animated widgets on the without a screenshot workaround. Festivitas for Mac requires some accessibility access to work. I asked Støvring about Apple's planned permission changes in macOS 27.3, and how they will affect the Festivitas app. He said Festivitas gets far more access than it needs because Apple's options aren't granular enough, and he'd prefer to ask for less access. Menu bar lights, snow, and pointer effects work without the System & App Protection Override permission, while lights in the Dock and snow landing on windows require access. Festivitas for the Mac offers customer-chosen fair pricing

items.title: Meta's Muse AI Agent Comes to Instagram DMs
items.summary: Meta today expanded what Muse can do in Instagram, making the personal AI agent more useful. Muse can organize the Instagram content you save into collections or travel itineraries, plus it can make grocery lists for recipes you find. Meta says you can also chat with Muse in DMs to learn more about…
items.body: Meta today expanded what Muse can do in Instagram, making the personal AI agent more useful. Muse can organize the Instagram content you save into collections or travel itineraries, plus it can make grocery lists for recipes you find. Meta says you can also chat with Muse in DMs to learn more about a post or catch up on what you've missed. When saving a post on Instagram, users in the U.S. and Canada will see an option to have Muse organize their posts. Muse in DMs will show up as a standard conversation. As TechCrunch points out, Muse for Instagram DMs lets users chat with the AI agent without having to switch from Instagram to the Muse app and back again. Conversations with Muse on Instagram will also appear as a side chat in the Muse app. Muse won't make changes or take actions without user permission. Muse support for Instagram DMs is rolling out in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore starting today.
